title: Spending on others
hook: spending on others lifted happiness more than spending on oneself (Dunn, Aknin and Norton)

segments.voice: Yesterday: be the one. The smoke room, the calm actors, and the choice to move first. Were you the one, even in something small? Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

An envelope, a little cash, and a slip of paper with one instruction. On a university campus, researchers handed these to people in the morning. Some slips said: spend this on yourself by five o'clock today. A bill, a treat, a gift for you. Others said: spend it on someone else, or give it to charity. That evening, each person got a phone call and one question. How happy are you feeling right now? Before hearing the answer, a guess: which slip sounds like the happier day?
screen: `AN ENVELOPE OF CASH.` → `SPEND IT BY FIVE.` → `ON YOU, OR ON SOMEONE ELSE?`

segments.voice: First, the study. Psychologists Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton ran that envelope experiment. People were told, at random, to spend the money on themselves or on others. Second, the result. In the evening, the people who had spent on others reported feeling happier than the people who had spent on themselves. And how much was in the envelope mattered less than where the money went. Third, the twist. The researchers also asked a separate group to predict the outcome. Those people mostly guessed the opposite: that spending on yourself would make you happier, and that more money would matter most. Our own forecasts about what will make us glad can be off. Fourth, older voices. In the Acts of the Apostles, Paul reminds a gathering of the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, in the King James Version: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." In the Pali texts, when the Buddha gives his step-by-step talk to a newcomer, the first topic is giving, called dana. Two paths, each with its own reasons, and each putting giving near the heart of a good life. The science is smaller and plainer than the scriptures. It just measured a mood at the end of an ordinary day. But it found the same direction: a little of what you have, spent for someone else, came back that evening as a happier answer on the phone.
screen: `AN ENVELOPE, AT RANDOM.` · `GIVERS WERE HAPPIER.` · then, large: `MOST GUESSED WRONG.` · then: `MORE BLESSED TO GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: buy something small for someone. Sit and let the breath settle. Then bring three people to mind: someone close, someone at work or school, someone you barely know. For each, picture one small thing you could get them today: a coffee, a pastry, a flower, a bus fare, a donation in their name. Nothing grand. Choose one. See yourself handing it over, and notice what happens in your chest as you picture it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Spending on others. In one study, people told to spend a little money on someone else ended the day happier than those who spent it on themselves. Today's word.
Your line: for someone else. Today, spend one small amount for someone else, and tonight, before sleep, check in on your own mood. Day one thousand three hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Giving is a practice in Christianity and Buddhism alike: Christians recall Jesus' words that it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), and in the Buddha's graduated talk, dana, generosity, is the first topic; some people set aside a small amount each week to spend on others.

notes: The index hook cites 2008; the year and dollar amounts are dropped under the claims rule.

Confirm study details: participants on campus received an envelope in the morning, were randomly assigned to spend on themselves or on others/charity by 5 pm, and reported happiness that evening; spending on others led to higher happiness; amount did not significantly matter.
Confirm that a separate group predicted the opposite (personal spending and the larger amount would bring more happiness), and that 'mostly guessed' is fair.
Confirm that the graduated talk (anupubbi-katha) begins with giving, as the script now says in place of 'often the first practice taught'.
Confirm KJV Acts 20:35 wording for the quoted clause.

Editor pass: hook moved from a second-person staged-study opener (third in four days) to a third-person object opener; cut the 'slightly bigger treat' line (the amounts differed more than slightly); replaced 'dana is often the first practice taught' with the graduated talk, which the source names; swapped the closing 'something money can't buy' uplift and the 'many traditions' claim.
